title: Invariant Features in Language Models: Geometric Characterization and Model Attribution
claim: Equivalent inputs converge to compact local regions whose geometry separates nuisance from semantic directions, enabling downstream model identification.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, dotted rounded boxes with bold arrows between
description: Three dotted rounded panels read left to right, joined by bold arrows. Panel A, Meaning Convergence, stacks three paraphrase bubbles ("A man is riding a horse" and two variants). An arrow leads to a sketch of stacked blocks with a dashed ellipse holding dark dots, labeled Invariant Features. Panel B, Local Geometric Interpretation, shows a curved manifold grid with a cluster of spheres at point z. Two arrows, V_nuisance and V_semantic, point away from it. The label Invariant Zone sits below, with the tangent-space decomposition T_zM = T^sem ⊕ T^nuis. Panel C, Discovery and Attribution, is a small flowchart. An activation cube feeds Activations, then Geometric Decomposition (with a generalized eigenvalue equation), then Discover Invariant Zones. That box leads to LLM 1 and LLM 2 fingerprint icons, and then to Model Attribution. Each panel ends with a one-line caption. The palette is mostly grayscale.
caption: Emergence of invariant semantic regions in LLMs. (A) Paraphrases propagate through layers and tend to converge to compact zones. (B) Local geometric interpretation: nuisance vs semantic tangent directions. (C) Geometric decomposition detects invariant zones for model attribution.
abstract: Language models exhibit strong robustness to paraphrasing, suggesting that semantic information may be encoded through stable internal representations, yet the structure and origin of such invariance remain unclear. We propose a local geometric framework in which semantically equivalent inputs produce representations that occupy structured regions in latent space, with paraphrastic variation along nuisance directions and semantic identity preserved in invariant subspaces. Building on this view, we make three contributions: (1) a geometric characterization of invariant latent features, (2) a contrastive subspace discovery method that separates semantic-changing from semantic-preserving variation, and (3) an application of invariant representations to zero-shot model attribution. Across models and layers, empirical results support these contributions. Invariant structure emerges in specific depth regions, semantic displacement lies largely outside the nuisance subspace, and representation-level interventions indicate a causal role of invariant components in model outputs. Invariant representations also capture model-specific geometric patterns, enabling accurate attribution. Together, these findings support a local geometric characterization of semantic invariance in language model representations.
